text: I think one important thing to know about Chinese and East Asian cuisine in general is that texture is far more important than in European and American cuisine. Asian people see texture as important as flavour. That’s why there are famous popular foods like mochi, bubble tea, and tteokbokki. Even though those ingredients in themselves have no flavour, they add TEXTURE. That’s also why some Asian foods might seem weird or scary, like fish bone marrow or chicken feet, but it’s because it’s impossible to achieve the same variety of texture just by eating plain old animal meat. Western cuisine focuses heavily on flavour but comparatively deprioritizes texture

Guys, I have a confession:

After following Jolly since like 2016, I realized something.

For some reason, I felt like Josh and Ollie are trying their best not to show JAPANESE stuff on their channel. I get that Jolly came from Korean Englishman, and that their main target are Korean and/or people who wants to know more about Korea.

However, listen to this:

For the past 4 years, we've had so many content from Jolly where they introduced us to a lot of different culture. Now, when we talk about Korean culture, we can thank Josh and Ollie for that.

In most recent years however, we get to know more about Asian culture in general through the lenses of Jolly. We got Malaysian from the collaboration with Uncle Roger, Indonesian with the Indomie flavor tasting, Indian with the Michelin Star content, Chinese with most recent video with them collaborating with David Beckham and now this; which is a great content. However, they left a big Asian country name out of the picture. Japan.

I get that Japan has already gotten a lot of attention from other creators such as Abroad in Japan and/or Trash Taste, but they're not Jolly. Or at least, not through the POV of Josh and Ollie.

At some point, if I'm not mistaken, I've watched a Jolly video or Korean Englishman where Josh introduced a "traditional" Korean comfort food to a guest, and the food was Tonkasseu ( Pork Cutlet ) to which the name itself is Japanese in origin ( At least, according to google) as to "Tonkatsu". I mean, what are the odds that Josh can be that ignorant over the fact that the food is actually not Korean in origin but of Japanese, yet he said that it was a Korean dish.

This is the reason why I kind of have an issue with Jolly team. Like, are they intentionally not making content about Japan yet somehow are only okay towards the other East Asian country ( Korean - Chinese ) and/or other Asian countries? I get that Korea and Japan still have some unresolved issue, but seriously? Even after almost a decade of making content, they never tried one of the biggest Asian culture? Japan?

I don't know about you guys, but this is something where I kind of felt off about Josh and Ollie. I feel like they intentionally left Japan on purpose despite the fact that Japan being one of the countries where you could reap a lot of content from.

I just realized that I was pretty spoiled when I was growing up, eating all those foods and taking it all for granted. The only thing I haven’t had is that fish marrow. But I love abalone and sea cucumber. We did have crab more often than we probably deserved. We used to have bird’s nest soup often, and it didn’t register in my kid mind what I was having, but I loved it (same with shark fin when we had family banquets). Certainly we had char siu and roast duck so often that I did sometimes get a bit sick of it, though that should be considered a crime. Chef Tam is amazingly talented, but funny and humble, such a great combination.

Even when Chinese food was purchased in little shops in Chinatown, they were mostly top-notch foods, and cheap! But things have gotten so expensive now. Still, the food is more affordable than other things, and the quality is exceptional at some places. It’s so nice to see the group eating and showcasing Chinese food from this region, because this food is my childhood. This experience hits very differently, and I’m glad they love it (especially Luke, his reactions are so precious).

text: I remember my first "fancy" dinner in China (Suzhou).  It was a welcome dinner for all the teachers at the beginning of the school term.  We walked into a very nice, large room akin to this one.  There was already an appetizer sitting at each place: a chicken's foot in an orange sauce.  Not a single foreign teacher touched theirs while our Chinese hosts were chowing down.  LOL  There were a couple of dishes that suited my palate, but I only nibbled here and there.  Luckily, there was a KFC just a few shops down for afterward!  Over the years, my taste buds grew more accustomed to local cuisine, but I still preferred street food and, I don't know, "comfort" food over the more elegant dishes.  My favorite to this day is niu rou chao mian (beef fried noodles).

Even in the ancient time, when Chinese emperor recruited the best chefs in China, there are more than 100 chefs working in the forbidden city. All of them are the best in their cuisine branch. And trust me, if you want authentic Chinese food, throw way so called Black Pearl Restaurant Guide, that's rubbish. Go different provinces of China, ask a local to introduce for you. And there are over a thousand of different dishes in Chinese cuisine, no one can master all of them. Some chef may only be the best at a certain dish and has been cooking and practicing for that with life long time. They probably don't work in a fancy restaurant, but for that certain dish of food, they are the best.
